title: Four virtues

cards: If character is the only good, what does it look like? Not in a sermon. On a Wednesday.
When the kid spills the juice, when the boss asks you to fudge a number, when the last slice of cake is looking at you. The Stoics didn't leave it vague.
They had a short list, four words long, inherited from Plato and turned into a daily tool. It would fit on a sticky note.

teach.b: Here they are. Wisdom: seeing clearly what's good, what's bad and what doesn't matter, and knowing what to do. Courage: doing the right thing when it's frightening or uncomfortable, and bearing what has to be borne.

Justice: treating people fairly and kindly, doing your part for the common good. And self-control, sometimes called temperance or moderation: wanting things in the right measure, not being dragged around by appetite.
The Greek word for that last one is sophrosyne, literally something like a sound mind, a safe and healthy way of thinking.

teach.h: NAMED BY PLATO, KEPT BY MANY.
teach.b: Plato had already named these four. Much later, Christian writers took them up as the cardinal virtues, from the Latin for a hinge: the virtues a good life swings on. Now the Stoic twist.
These aren't four separate skills you collect like badges.
They're one excellence seen from four sides, and you can't really have one without the others. Courage without justice: a bold thief. Is that courage?
The Stoics said no, that's just nerve. Justice without wisdom: meaning well and making a mess. Self-control without courage: a careful coward.

Each virtue needs the others to be itself. Marcus Aurelius, writing to himself, says that if he ever finds anything in life better than justice, truth, self-control and courage, he should turn to it with his whole soul.
It reads as a dare to himself, and the four still stand. That makes the list practical. In any moment, four questions: what's true here, what's brave, what's fair, and what's enough?

how: Modern Stoic practitioners often pick one of the four virtues as a focus for the day and review in the evening where it showed up or went missing.

games.q: the four virtues — tap the pairs.

s: for the Stoics, you could have courage without justice
they held the virtues come together; a bold thief only has nerve.
the four were already named by Plato
the Stoics inherited them and made them a daily tool.
cardinal comes from the Latin for a hinge
the virtues a good life swings on.

games.q: a thief is fearless and daring. would the Stoics call him courageous?
o: no, without justice it's just nerve.
only if he gets away with it.
games.why: for the Stoics the virtues are one excellence seen from four sides. courage without justice isn't the real thing.

practice: Run through the rest of today, its meetings, meals and messages, and hold up the four one at a time: wisdom, courage, justice, self-control.
Pick the one today most needs from you; if one makes you wince a little, that may be the answer. Say its name quietly on each out-breath.
